# Weekly Market Briefing: Positioning Through Factor Whiplash And Extreme Single-Stock Dispersion

The past week delivered one of the more violent bouts of factor and single-stock dispersion across our watchlist this year, with cloud infrastructure and select cyclicals ripping higher while much of software, fintech, and consumer internet extended an ongoing de‑rating. At the extremes, Fastly surged by about one hundred thirteen percent week on week, while Rapid7, Hims & Hers, monday.com, Pinterest, and a cluster of enterprise and fintech names fell by roughly twenty to thirty percent, underscoring how fragile positioning and sentiment remain across higher‑beta growth assets. Against this backdrop of sharp idiosyncratic moves but no near‑term earnings catalysts, the key portfolio question is whether we are seeing the early stages of a durable rotation within growth – toward profitable infrastructure and cyclicals – or a transient short‑covering rally and capitulation in the names that have led the drawdown in recent weeks.

## Market Overview

From a top‑down perspective, the week was defined less by broad index direction and more by cross‑currents beneath the surface, with unusually wide spreads between best and worst performers even within the same thematic buckets. Within software infrastructure, Fastly’s roughly one hundred thirteen percent weekly gain and near one hundred percent month‑over‑month move stood out as an extreme outlier, coinciding with positive positioning and short‑covering dynamics rather than any new fundamental data in the last few days. By contrast, application and workflow software continued to trade in “post‑peak growth” mode, with monday.com down about twenty six percent on the week and roughly forty four percent over the month, Freshworks off nearly nineteen percent on the week and about thirty seven percent over the month, and Asana lower by almost fourteen percent on the week and roughly thirty four percent over the month.

Across the broader technology complex, the pattern was one of investors rewarding profitability, visible cash flows, and real‑world leverage to infrastructure build‑out, while penalizing names perceived as longer duration, subscale, or still proving out their unit economics. Vertiv, a key beneficiary of data center and AI infrastructure demand, gained almost twenty percent on the week and about thirty seven percent over the month. Comfort Systems, another infrastructure and mechanical services beneficiary, climbed almost nine percent on the week and about twenty seven percent over the month, and Caterpillar posted a gain of roughly seven percent on the week and more than twenty percent on the month. On the materials side, Corning’s near nine percent weekly gain and almost forty eight percent monthly move highlighted how quickly sentiment can pivot when markets recognize an earnings and capital return inflection.

Financials, fintech, and parts of consumer underperformed in sympathy with ongoing concerns around the sustainability of the consumer and the potential for higher funding costs or tighter credit conditions. LPL Financial declined about thirteen percent on the week, Block slipped roughly eleven percent, and Affirm dropped almost thirteen percent, with monthly drawdowns of roughly ten percent, twenty four percent, and thirty one percent respectively. Large diversified banks on the watchlist also saw selling pressure, with Wells Fargo, Bank of America, JPMorgan, and Capital One posting weekly declines of roughly seven, seven, six, and seven percent respectively, even though their one‑month moves were less severe than those seen in higher‑beta fintech.

In this context, the underlying message of the week for portfolio construction is that markets remain unforgiving of any perceived duration, execution, or regulatory risk, while being willing to pay up quickly for tangible cash flow leverage to secular capex cycles. That means investors are increasingly differentiating within technology between infrastructure and applications, within fintech between scaled payments and unproven lending models, and within consumer between defensive staples and discretionary or advertising‑dependent platforms. The lack of near‑term earnings catalysts over the next two weeks, as indicated by the absence of watchlist earnings in that window, further concentrates price discovery into flows, factor moves, and any incremental macro headlines, amplifying volatility.

## Sector Leadership & Rotation

### Technology: Infrastructure Versus Applications

The clearest rotation this week occurred inside technology, particularly within software and infrastructure, where the bifurcation between profitable, scale infrastructure assets and longer‑duration application names widened further. In software infrastructure, Fastly’s approximately one hundred thirteen percent weekly gain and nearly ninety eight percent monthly move epitomized the violent snap‑back that can occur when heavily shorted names intersect with even modestly improving narratives around cost discipline and path to profit. Fastly’s move dwarfed already strong gains from Vertiv, which rose roughly twenty percent on the week and about thirty seven percent on the month, and Akamai, which gained about eighteen percent on the week and more than twenty three percent on the month. Cloudflare rounded out the group with a gain of roughly thirteen percent week on week and about four percent over the month, while Datadog and Ciena each delivered weekly gains of about twelve percent, with Datadog modestly positive on the month and Ciena up more than twenty seven percent.

This pattern within software infrastructure stands in stark contrast to the application layer, where selling pressure was notable and often indiscriminate. In application software, Hims & Hers fell by roughly twenty nine percent on the week and about forty eight percent over the month, monday.com declined about twenty six percent on the week and roughly forty four percent for the month, Freshworks dropped almost nineteen percent on the week and about thirty seven percent over the month, and Asana fell nearly fourteen percent on the week and about thirty four percent on the month. Cognizant and Tyler Technologies, both perceived as steadier IT and vertical software names, still lost approximately fourteen and thirteen percent on the week respectively, with monthly declines above twenty percent for both. Even IBM, viewed as a more defensive enterprise bellwether, slid about twelve percent week on week and roughly fifteen percent on the month, highlighting how broad the de‑rating has been across legacy and next‑generation enterprise software when investors question forward growth durability.

Oracle, however, bucked that negative application trend with a gain of roughly twelve percent on the week, despite being down more than seventeen percent over the past month. The stock’s weekly move underscores how quickly sentiment can reset when investors recalibrate cloud growth expectations, recognize the value of installed bases, or reassess capital return trajectories. More broadly, the divergence between Oracle’s weekly gain and the sharp drawdowns in high‑multiple SaaS and workflow names speaks to a shift in investor preference toward scaled platforms with perceived pricing power and embedded enterprise relationships, even if top‑line growth is less spectacular.

### Cybersecurity: From Capitulation To Selective Repair

Cybersecurity remained a locus of volatility, with the group showing both sharp downside and pockets of recovery. Rapid7 was the most notable casualty, falling roughly thirty four percent on the week and about forty seven percent over the month. The magnitude of that drawdown, especially in a week without fresh earnings, points to a mix of disappointing prior guidance, competitive and margin concerns, and a market that increasingly demands clear profitability roadmaps in security as in broader software. Hims & Hers, although technically in health tech rather than pure cybersecurity, experienced a similar magnitude of investor de‑risking, reinforcing the theme of markets penalizing perceived long‑duration equity stories without near‑term cash flow visibility.

Other cybersecurity names fared better but still displayed dispersion reflective of investors differentiating by scale, profitability, and exposure to next‑generation security architectures. Varonis gained about twelve percent on the week but remained down roughly twenty seven percent over the month, suggesting that the recent bounce may be more of a technical mean reversion after a sharp prior de‑rating than a decisive shift in the fundamental narrative. CrowdStrike rose roughly nine percent on the week but was still down about seven percent on the month, while Rubrik gained nearly seven percent on the week despite being roughly twenty percent lower over the month, reinforcing the idea that recent IPOs and high‑growth names are still in the process of finding durable valuation floors.

Tenable and Zscaler each advanced by about six percent on the week, with Tenable roughly flat over the month and Zscaler still down about seventeen percent, while Qualys and Check Point declined by approximately five percent week on week and high single digits over the month. Overall, the security space looks like it is transitioning from broad‑based derating to a more selective regime, where platforms with clear cloud‑native architectures, endpoint dominance, or privileged identity stories are stabilizing, while names still scaling or perceived as point products face ongoing scrutiny. From a portfolio construction standpoint, this favors a barbell between high‑quality, profitable leaders such as CrowdStrike and more idiosyncratic turnaround or M&A candidates like Rapid7, albeit sized carefully given volatility.

### Semiconductors And AI: Sorting Winners From Tourists

Semiconductors had a mixed week, reflecting both ongoing enthusiasm for AI infrastructure and a more discriminating approach to the broader semi complex. Astera Labs fell by roughly twenty four percent on the week and about twenty five percent over the month, a notable underperformance that likely reflects its status as a recent high‑expectation AI infrastructure IPO and the market’s current unwillingness to underwrite extended duration without near‑term execution proof. Intel also declined by about eight percent on the week and roughly four percent on the month, consistent with lingering concerns around foundry competitiveness, capex intensity, and the pace of margin recovery.

By contrast, Credo Technology rose about nine percent on the week, even though it remains down roughly twenty three percent on the month, and Tower Semiconductor fell by about seven percent on the week but is still modestly positive, roughly four to five percent, over the month. Cadence gained approximately six percent on the week with a modest mid‑single‑digit decline over the month, while Taiwan Semiconductor rose about five percent over the week and roughly twelve percent on the month. The underlying message is that markets continue to favor the “picks and shovels” of the AI cycle – design tools, leading‑edge foundry capacity, and high‑value connectivity – while scrutinizing more speculative or recently listed names that came to market with AI narratives.

### AdTech, Media, And Consumer Internet: Weakness Beneath The Surface

Advertising‑linked and consumer internet names on the watchlist struggled, adding another leg to a multi‑week de‑rating in parts of this cohort. Pinterest declined by roughly twenty one percent on the week and about forty three percent on the month, a very significant reset that suggests concerns around user growth, engagement trends, or monetization efficiency have combined with an overall risk‑off backdrop in ad‑driven models. Sprinklr and Zeta each fell by about eight to nine percent on the week and roughly twenty three to thirty one percent on the month, while Netflix declined by about six and a half percent on the week and more than thirteen percent on the month.

In the broader digital commerce and web infrastructure space, GigaCloud dropped roughly twelve to thirteen percent on the week and about fourteen percent on the month, GoDaddy declined about eight percent on the week and almost eighteen percent on the month, and Wix lost roughly eight percent week on week and about twenty one percent on the month. By contrast, RAMP gained about five percent on the week while The Trade Desk was lower by around four to five percent, and APP fell roughly four percent. The overall pattern is one where investors are de‑risking non‑essential consumer and advertising exposure, particularly in names where valuation still embeds healthy growth expectations, while showing more willingness to differentiate among platforms with greater visibility on user and revenue growth.

### Financials And Fintech: Pro‑Cyclical But Out Of Favor

Within financials, the watchlist saw broad weakness across both traditional banks and newer fintech platforms. LPL’s roughly thirteen percent weekly drawdown, combined with a ten percent monthly slide, pointed to concerns around flows, margin compression, or potential regulatory and policy uncertainties related to advice and brokerage economics. Among pure‑play fintech names, Affirm’s approximately thirteen percent weekly decline and roughly thirty one percent monthly slide, Block’s eleven percent weekly drop and about twenty four percent monthly loss, and Shift4’s seven percent weekly and roughly eighteen percent monthly declines highlight how the market is demanding demonstrable profitability, resilient unit economics, and clear differentiation in a crowded field.

The diversified banks on the watchlist – Wells Fargo, Bank of America, JPMorgan, and Capital One – each fell between roughly six and seven percent on the week, though their one‑month moves, near flat to mid‑single‑digit declines, are much less extreme than those in smaller fintechs. This pattern suggests that investors see more fundamental support in scaled, deposit‑funded universal banks but remain worried about net interest margins, loan growth, and credit costs. At the same time, the weak performance of consumer‑focused financials such as Synchrony, which declined about five percent on the week and more than eight percent on the month, signals continued caution around lower‑income and non‑prime consumers.

### Energy, Industrials, And Materials: Quiet Outperformance

The strongest relative performance this week came from energy, industrials, and select materials, confirming that investors are still willing to own names levered to real‑asset cycles, capex, and potential inflation hedges. Generac’s roughly twenty two percent weekly gain and forty percent monthly move stand out, reinforcing the narrative of rising demand for distributed generation and backup power solutions, especially as grid stability, extreme weather, and data center power loads move to the forefront of policy and corporate agendas. Vertiv’s nearly twenty percent weekly and about thirty seven percent monthly gains underscore similar themes in data center infrastructure, where power and thermal management are seeing structurally higher demand.

Sable Offshore rose about twelve percent on the week, though it remains down over twenty percent on the month, while Comfort Systems gained nearly nine percent on the week and about twenty seven percent over the month. In materials, Agnico Eagle and Newmont gained about ten and nine percent on the week respectively, with roughly ten percent monthly gains for both, consistent with stronger precious metals pricing and investor demand for perceived hedges. Corning’s near nine percent weekly and almost forty eight percent monthly gains highlight the market’s growing appreciation of its leverage to data, display, and specialty materials cycles. The broader takeaway is that real‑asset‑linked names are increasingly acting as a counterweight to growth volatility within diversified portfolios.

## Top Movers & Earnings Recap

### Extreme Winners: Fastly, Generac, Vertiv, And Corning

Fastly’s approximately one hundred thirteen percent weekly surge and nearly ninety eight percent monthly gain made it the standout winner on the entire watchlist. The move reflects an intense confluence of factors: an elevated short base built up over a long period of fundamental skepticism, a still‑credible longer‑term narrative around edge computing and security, and, likely, incremental signs of cost discipline and operational focus. The magnitude of the move in a single week is hard to reconcile with any plausible one‑week change in long‑term fundamentals, which suggests that positioning and technicals played a dominant role. For long‑only investors, this kind of spike after a deep drawdown presents a classic challenge: whether to view the move as an opportunity to take profits and redeploy into earlier‑stage turnarounds, or as confirmation that the worst is over and the multiple can re‑rate closer to scaled cloud peers over time.

Generac’s roughly twenty two percent weekly gain and forty percent monthly move represent a powerful confirmation of investor willingness to revisit cyclical and infrastructure‑linked names when the earnings and demand narratives inflect. After a period where the stock was pressured by concerns over post‑pandemic demand normalization and inventory, the recent performance suggests that investors are again assigning value to its leverage to grid reliability, distributed power, and backup generation. The outperformance relative to many software and fintech names also underscores the degree to which the market currently prefers visible earnings and cash flows tied to physical infrastructure and decarbonization‑adjacent themes.

Vertiv, with its approximately twenty percent weekly and roughly thirty seven percent monthly gains, sits at the intersection of these themes. The stock has become a high‑conviction expression of the AI and cloud infrastructure investment wave, given its exposure to power, cooling, and critical data center infrastructure. The magnitude and consistency of the recent move suggest that investors increasingly see Vertiv as a structural winner rather than a purely cyclical beneficiary. For portfolios, this kind of name becomes central not only as a direct AI infrastructure play, but also as a diversifier against more speculative AI software and semiconductor exposures.

Corning’s near nine percent weekly and almost forty eight percent monthly gain is another important datapoint. After years of muted sentiment and concerns about display cycles and smartphone demand, the stock’s recent performance indicates that the market is re‑rating its role in optical communications, specialty glass, and other high‑value materials tied to data, automotive, and consumer electronics. The strong monthly move, in particular, suggests that investors have moved from trading the name tactically around near‑term cycles to viewing it as a more strategic compounder with improving capital returns.

### Extreme Losers: Rapid7, Hims & Hers, monday.com, Pinterest, And Friends

On the downside, Rapid7’s roughly thirty four percent weekly and nearly forty seven percent monthly decline was among the worst across the watchlist, signaling a marked loss of confidence in the company’s medium‑term trajectory. In the context of cybersecurity, where leading platforms such as CrowdStrike, Zscaler, and others have proven that scale and cloud‑native architectures can support strong growth and expanding margins, investors appear increasingly unwilling to underwrite security names that sit outside that leadership cluster without a clear and credible path to margin and cash flow improvement. Rapid7’s drawdown likely reflects a mix of prior guidance disappointments, concerns around product breadth versus deeper platform peers, and a market that is less willing to pay for revenue growth in isolation.

Hims & Hers, down approximately twenty nine percent on the week and about forty eight percent on the month, fits a related pattern, albeit in health tech. The company’s direct‑to‑consumer model, digital health proposition, and brand have delivered strong top‑line growth historically, but the recent drawdown suggests investors are questioning the sustainability of marketing efficiency, unit economics, and competitive moats, especially as the space becomes more crowded and regulatory scrutiny increases. The magnitude of the monthly move implies that the stock has transitioned in investor perception from a high‑growth disruptor to a more speculative long‑duration asset, at least for now.

monday.com’s roughly twenty six percent weekly and about forty four percent monthly declines underscore just how quickly sentiment can reverse even on high‑quality, widely used SaaS platforms when investors reassess growth durability, competitive intensity, or margin trajectories. Freshworks, Asana, Tyler Technologies, and Cognizant, all down by roughly thirteen to nineteen percent this week and more than twenty percent on the month, reinforce the narrative that the market is repricing the entire cohort of workflow, IT services, and vertical software names where growth is decelerating from pandemic‑era highs and valuation multiples still embed healthy expectations. The question for long‑only investors is how to distinguish between transient sentiment swings and genuine shifts in the growth and profitability outlook.

Pinterest’s approximately twenty one percent weekly and about forty three percent monthly drawdown stands out in the ad‑supported consumer space. Its recent weakness likely reflects fears around competition for ad dollars amid macro uncertainty, platform‑specific engagement questions, and possibly concerns about how quickly newer ad products and formats can scale. With Netflix also lower by roughly six to seven percent on the week and more than thirteen percent on the month, and a cohort of adtech names such as Sprinklr and Zeta down high single digits weekly and over twenty percent monthly, the sector appears firmly in the penalty box for now.

### Earnings And Corporate News Flow: A Quiet Period

The coming two weeks include no earnings from names on our watchlist, which means the market has entered a relatively quiet period on the company‑specific fundamental front. That amplifies the role of macro headlines, sector flows, and technical positioning in driving price action. The sharp moves in names like Fastly, Rapid7, Hims & Hers, and monday.com this week, absent incremental earnings, illustrate how impactful non‑fundamental drivers can be when valuations are elevated, positioning is crowded, or narratives are fragile.

In this environment, any incremental corporate news – for example, mid‑quarter updates, analyst days, product launches, or regulatory developments – can be disproportionately impactful. However, with no scheduled earnings on the near‑term calendar, investors are likely to continue anchoring on prior quarter results and guidance, adjusting positions primarily based on changes in macro expectations, factor performance, and comparative valuations within sectors. That increases the importance of patience, liquidity management, and disciplined sizing, especially in higher‑beta names.

## Macro & Rates Environment

With no fresh macro data embedded in our dataset for the week, we focus on the qualitative ways in which the evolving rates and policy backdrop are interacting with sector performance on our watchlist. The prevailing regime remains one of elevated but increasingly data‑dependent policy, where central banks are balancing the risks of lingering inflation with concerns about growth momentum and financial stability. For equities, particularly growth and long‑duration assets, the central question remains how stable investors perceive the real rate environment to be and how quickly policy might shift if growth data softens.

The underperformance of fintech, consumer credit, and parts of discretionary and advertising‑exposed names is consistent with a market that remains wary of the cumulative impact of higher funding costs on households and small businesses. Names like Affirm, Block, and Synchrony, which are directly tied to consumer credit dynamics and discretionary spending, sold off notably this week, suggesting that investors are not yet ready to price in a benign credit cycle or a rapid easing in policy. Similarly, the weakness in large banks such as Wells Fargo, Bank of America, JPMorgan, and Capital One indicates ongoing concern around net interest margins, deposit competition, and the shape of the yield curve, even if the selloff is less severe than in higher‑beta fintech.

At the same time, the outperformance of real‑asset and infrastructure‑linked sectors such as energy, industrials, and materials – including Generac, Vertiv, Comfort Systems, Corning, Agnico Eagle, and Newmont – suggests that investors continue to see value in exposures that can benefit from nominal growth, potential inflation resilience, and structural capex cycles. These sectors are perceived as better positioned to pass through cost pressures, sustain pricing power, and generate cash flows that are less sensitive to modest changes in discount rates. In practice, that means portfolios are increasingly using these names both as offensive plays on infrastructure and as defensive ballast against drawdowns in higher‑duration technology and consumer assets.

For software and long‑duration growth, the interplay with rates has been especially evident in the sharp de‑ratings observed in application software, cybersecurity names without clear profitability paths, and health and consumer tech platforms reliant on external funding or aggressive reinvestment. monday.com, Freshworks, Asana, Hims & Hers, Rapid7, and others that saw weekly declines in the mid‑teens to high‑twenties percent, with similar or worse monthly moves, exemplify the market’s reluctance to underwrite multiyear growth stories without evidence of unit economic resilience and margin expansion. Even higher‑quality names such as Intuit, which fell about ten percent on the week and nearly thirty percent on the month, and Atlassian, which declined about eleven percent on the week and roughly thirty six percent on the month, are not immune when valuation starting points are rich.

Against this backdrop, investors appear to be favoring a barbell strategy within growth: on one side, AI and cloud infrastructure plays with near‑term earnings leverage such as Vertiv, Corning, and Taiwan Semiconductor; on the other, large, profitable platforms across software, payments, and internet that can sustain growth even in a slower macro environment. While some of these larger names on the broader watchlist, such as Amazon and Alphabet, were down around five percent on the week and mid‑ to high‑single‑digit percentages on the month, they still represent core holdings for many portfolios given their diversified revenue bases and balance sheet strength. The current challenge is sizing those exposures in a way that acknowledges near‑term volatility without losing the long‑term compounding potential those businesses offer.

## Watchlist Deep Dives

### Fastly (FSLY): From Deep Value To Momentum Darling In A Week

Fastly’s roughly one hundred thirteen percent gain this week and nearly ninety eight percent move over the month transformed it from a heavily shorted, structurally questioned name into one of the market’s most visible momentum stories. The company has long sat at the intersection of content delivery, edge computing, and security, but it has struggled to convert that technological positioning into consistent revenue growth and profitability. Prior quarters have been marked by uneven execution, periodic guidance resets, and debates around whether it can compete effectively against larger CDNs and hyperscalers that increasingly integrate similar capabilities.

The recent move appears to be driven less by a step‑change in fundamentals and more by a combination of improved narrative and positioning. Any incremental signs that Fastly can rationalize costs, improve go‑to‑market efficiency, or stabilize churn can catalyze outsized price moves when the short interest is high and buy‑side positioning is underweight. For long‑only investors, the key questions now are how much of the near‑term upside has simply pulled forward future returns, and whether the company can sustain the kind of revenue growth and margin expansion that current price action is starting to embed.

From a portfolio perspective, Fastly’s new profile is more akin to a high‑beta tactical position than a core holding until there is sustained evidence of execution. The volatility implied by a one‑week doubling in the share price argues for modest position sizes, tight risk controls, and a clearly articulated thesis around either a fundamental inflection or a potential strategic scenario. At the same time, the move is an important reminder that deeply de‑rated infrastructure names with real assets and customers can become powerful performers if they show credible progress toward profitability.

### Rapid7 (RPD): A Case Study In Security De‑rating

Rapid7’s roughly thirty four percent weekly and nearly forty seven percent monthly declines encapsulate the challenges facing mid‑tier security vendors in the current environment. The company competes in vulnerability management, detection and response, and security analytics, but it lacks the endpoint dominance of CrowdStrike or the zero‑trust branding of Zscaler, leaving it in a more crowded and competitive segment of the market. Recent quarters have seen increasing investor concern about growth deceleration, pricing pressure, and the gap between Rapid7’s margin profile and that of more scaled peers.

The magnitude of the recent drawdown suggests that investors are recalibrating their expectations for both growth and valuation, moving Rapid7 closer to the “show me” bucket where only clear evidence of sustainable margin expansion and free cash flow improvement can drive re‑rating. In addition, the security space has seen a wave of platformization, with larger vendors cross‑selling adjacent products and consolidating customer budgets, which may be pressuring standalone vendors without distinctive moats. The risk is that Rapid7 finds itself squeezed on both growth and margins, which would warrant further multiple compression.

For portfolios, the decision around Rapid7 revolves around whether to view the current valuation as discounting too bleak an outcome and thus presenting a contrarian opportunity, or as a value trap amid structural headwinds. The steep monthly decline raises the possibility of strategic interest from larger security or infrastructure players seeking to expand their product suites, but such outcomes are speculative. Until there is clarity on the company’s ability to reaccelerate or stabilize growth while lifting margins, most conservative investors are likely to stay cautious.

### Hims & Hers (HIMS): Re‑Rating A Direct‑To‑Consumer Growth Story

Hims & Hers, down roughly twenty nine percent on the week and about forty eight percent on the month, highlights how quickly sentiment can reverse for direct‑to‑consumer growth stories once investors reposition around risk. The company’s model, which combines telehealth, subscription services, and consumer branding across categories such as mental health, men’s health, and dermatology, has delivered impressive top‑line growth, but questions around long‑term unit economics and competitive dynamics have persisted. Marketing intensity, customer acquisition costs, and churn are all critical variables that markets reassess aggressively when risk appetite shifts.

The recent drawdown likely reflects a combination of valuation starting point, concerns about the sustainability of recent growth rates, and a broader shift away from long‑duration speculative growth. With health tech facing ongoing regulatory and reimbursement uncertainties, investors appear to be demanding clearer paths to durable profitability and lower volatility in user and revenue metrics. For Hims & Hers, that means any missteps or even modest disappointments in growth metrics can drive outsized share price reactions.

From a positioning standpoint, the stock now sits in a more speculative growth bucket. For investors willing to underwrite continued category expansion, strong consumer brand resonance, and improving margins over time, the current drawdown could represent an entry point. However, the volatility implied by a nearly fifty percent monthly move lower suggests that position sizes must be controlled, and the thesis must be revisited frequently in light of evolving competition and regulatory dynamics.

### monday.com (MNDY): High‑Quality SaaS Meets Multiple Compression

monday.com’s approximately twenty six percent weekly and about forty four percent monthly declines are striking given the company’s reputation as a high‑quality, product‑driven SaaS platform with strong growth. The stock has historically traded at a premium multiple on the back of rapid adoption, expanding use cases, and a strong product experience. However, as growth inevitably moderates from earlier levels and competition intensifies across collaboration, project management, and workflow automation, investors have become more sensitive to any perceived inflection points in demand or margins.

The recent drawdown appears to reflect a combination of multiple compression across high‑growth SaaS, concerns about macro‑driven IT budget caution, and a broader investor shift toward profitability and free cash flow. Even if monday.com continues to grow at a healthy rate, the bar set by prior valuation levels may no longer be sustainable in a world where the risk‑free rate is higher and investors demand clearer near‑term returns. This dynamic is not unique to monday.com but is especially visible given the stock’s prior outperformance.

In portfolios, monday.com remains a name where many investors will want exposure over the long term but may choose to scale in gradually, using volatility as an opportunity to build positions at more reasonable valuations. The key will be tracking whether enterprise adoption remains strong, whether expansion within existing customers holds up, and whether the company can continue to drive operating leverage even as it invests in product and go‑to‑market.

### Vertiv (VRT): A Premier Beneficiary Of Data Center And AI Capex

Vertiv’s roughly twenty percent weekly and about thirty seven percent monthly gains cement its status as one of the clearest ways to express the data center and AI infrastructure capex cycle in public markets. The company provides critical power, cooling, and infrastructure solutions for data centers, telecom, and industrial applications. As cloud providers, hyperscalers, and enterprises race to deploy AI training and inference capacity, the demand for high‑density power and advanced thermal management has surged, and Vertiv has been a direct beneficiary.

The stock’s recent performance reflects both earnings upgrades and a re‑rating of the multiple as investors increasingly view Vertiv as a structural winner rather than a cyclical capital goods name. The parallels with prior cycles in networking or storage are instructive: companies that sit at bottleneck points in a major capex cycle often enjoy several years of strong demand and pricing power, though they must manage supply chains, execution risk, and potential overbuild cycles. Vertiv’s challenge will be to meet demand without sacrificing margins or overextending on capacity and working capital.

For portfolios, the question is less whether to own Vertiv and more about sizing and time horizon. Given the strength of recent performance, new capital may prefer to enter on pullbacks rather than chase, but under‑owning the name in a world of structurally higher AI‑related capex carries its own opportunity cost. Vertiv also serves as a useful hedge against disappointment in more speculative AI software or semiconductor names, providing a tangible earnings stream tied to the same secular theme.

### Generac (GNRC): Re‑Emerging As A Structural Power Play

Generac’s roughly twenty two percent weekly and forty percent monthly gains underscore its re‑emergence as a structural play on distributed generation, grid reliability, and the electrification of demand. After a period in which the market focused heavily on post‑pandemic normalization of residential generator demand and inventory overhangs, investors are refocusing on long‑term drivers such as grid instability, extreme weather, and the growing power needs of data centers and electric vehicles.

The recent performance suggests that earnings expectations have been reset to more achievable levels and that investors now see upside risk if demand for backup and distributed power solutions accelerates. In addition, any incremental traction in new product areas or services, including grid‑interactive solutions or partnerships with utilities and data center operators, could further extend the growth runway. However, the stock’s cyclicality and sensitivity to macro and housing trends mean that volatility will remain a feature, not a bug.

Within diversified portfolios, Generac fits well alongside Vertiv and Corning as part of a real‑asset and infrastructure cluster that benefits from secular trends around data, power, and resilience. It also offers some diversification against pure energy commodity exposure, given its more equipment‑ and solutions‑driven revenue mix.

### Corning (GLW): From Cyclical To Structural In The Market’s Eyes

Corning’s nearly nine percent weekly and almost forty eight percent monthly gains reflect a decisive shift in how the market is viewing its role in the technology and industrial ecosystem. Historically, the stock has been treated largely as a cyclical play on display, consumer electronics, and to a lesser extent optical communications. Recently, however, investors appear to be assigning greater value to its exposure to multiple structural growth drivers, including data center and 5G fiber, advanced automotive glass, and specialty materials for consumer devices.

The strong monthly move suggests not only that earnings expectations have improved, but also that the market is willing to pay a higher multiple for Corning’s cash flows as it demonstrates better capital allocation and margin performance. In many portfolios, Corning can serve as a lower‑volatility complement to more volatile AI and semiconductor exposures, providing leverage to similar themes via materials rather than components. The key risk remains the inherent cyclicality of some end markets, but the recent price action indicates that investors now see the long‑term structural story as more important than near‑term cyclical noise.

### CrowdStrike (CRWD): High‑Quality Security With Renewed Volatility

CrowdStrike’s roughly nine percent weekly gain, despite a modest mid‑single‑digit monthly decline, highlights how investors continue to treat it as a core holding in cybersecurity even amid broader volatility. The company’s cloud‑native endpoint platform, strong customer momentum, and expanding product suite have consistently placed it at the top of security investors’ preference lists. The recent volatility appears more a function of broader software de‑rating and risk‑off flows than any fundamental deterioration.

For long‑term portfolios, CrowdStrike remains a key way to gain exposure to secular security spending growth, particularly as enterprises consolidate vendors and prioritize integrated platforms. The balance between growth and profitability, combined with a strong net retention profile, makes it relatively resilient compared to smaller or less differentiated peers. The main challenge for new capital is entry point after prior strong performance; using market‑wide pullbacks in high‑growth technology as opportunities to build positions remains a rational strategy.

### Oracle (ORCL): Value Within The Cloud And Database Complex

Oracle’s approximately twelve percent weekly gain, despite a roughly seventeen percent monthly decline, reflects the market’s search for relative value within the cloud, database, and enterprise software complex. While not a new economy darling, Oracle’s massive installed base, mission‑critical database products, and growing cloud infrastructure and application offerings give it leverage to multiple secular themes. The recent bounce may indicate that investors see its valuation as more grounded relative to high‑multiple SaaS names that have sold off sharply.

In portfolios, Oracle often serves as a “value within growth” holding, providing exposure to digital transformation, cloud migration, and AI workloads without the same level of valuation risk as earlier‑stage software names. The trade‑off is slower top‑line growth compared to pure‑play SaaS, but in the current environment of multiple compression and heightened focus on cash flows, that may be a feature rather than a flaw. Going forward, investor attention will focus on the pace of cloud adoption, the company’s ability to sustain margins, and the evolution of capital returns.

### Vertically Focused Software: Tyler Technologies (TYL) And Roper (ROP)

Tyler Technologies and Roper, down roughly thirteen and eleven percent respectively on the week and more than twenty percent over the month, exemplify the pressure on vertical and industrial software names that had been treated as quasi‑bond proxies. Their business models, focused on mission‑critical vertical applications with recurring revenue, have historically supported premium multiples and relatively low volatility. However, in an environment where risk‑free rates are higher and investors re‑price duration across all assets, even high‑quality, defensive software is not immune.

The recent drawdowns suggest that market participants are re‑evaluating how much of a premium to pay for stable, recurring software cash flows relative to other defensive sectors such as consumer staples or utilities, and relative to more cyclically geared industrials that now offer better earnings leverage at lower multiples. For portfolios, the key decision is whether to lean into these drawdowns as opportunities to acquire durable compounding franchises at more reasonable prices, or to reallocate toward higher‑beta names where valuation resets have been even more dramatic.

### Fintech: LPL (LPLA), Block (XYZ), Affirm (AFRM), And Global Payments (GPN)

Within fintech, LPL’s roughly thirteen percent weekly and ten percent monthly decline, Block’s approximately eleven percent weekly and twenty four percent monthly drop, Affirm’s roughly thirteen percent weekly and thirty one percent monthly fall, and Global Payments’ roughly six percent weekly and nearly twelve percent monthly decline paint a picture of a sector under pressure. Funding costs, regulatory uncertainty, competitive intensity, and evolving consumer behavior are all part of the narrative weighing on these names.

LPL, tied closely to wealth management flows and market levels, is particularly sensitive to investor risk appetite and the regulatory outlook for advice. Block and Affirm sit at the intersection of consumer spending, credit risk, and payments innovation, making them more vulnerable when markets question the sustainability of discretionary spending or the resilience of consumer credit. Global Payments, while more scaled and diversified, still reflects investor concerns about pricing, competition, and the broader health of transaction volumes.

For portfolios, the common thread is that fintech exposure must be carefully calibrated to one’s macro view on consumer health and rates. In more defensive stances, investors may tilt toward scaled payments networks and away from consumer credit‑exposed or less profitable platforms. In more constructive macro scenarios, the recent drawdowns could offer entry points into select names with strong competitive advantages and clear profitability paths.

### Semis: Astera Labs (ALAB), Intel (INTC), Credo (CRDO), Tower (TSEM), Cadence (CDNS), And TSMC (TSM)

Astera Labs’ roughly twenty four percent weekly and about twenty five percent monthly decline illustrates the difficulty of sustaining elevated valuations for newly public AI infrastructure names in a choppy market. While its positioning in connectivity solutions for AI and cloud workloads is compelling, the market appears unwilling to pay peak multiples without a longer track record of execution and earnings. Intel’s roughly eight percent weekly and four percent monthly decline reflects persistent concerns around its turnaround path, competitive dynamics, and capital intensity.

By contrast, Credo’s roughly nine percent weekly gain, despite a roughly twenty three percent monthly decline, and Tower’s roughly seven percent weekly decline alongside a modestly positive monthly move, underscore the market’s nuanced approach to smaller and specialty semis. Cadence’s roughly six percent weekly decline and modest mid‑single‑digit monthly pullback suggest that EDA and design software remain relatively resilient, while Taiwan Semiconductor’s roughly five percent weekly and about twelve percent monthly gains underscore its central role as a global foundry and key beneficiary of AI and advanced node demand.

For portfolios, the takeaway is that within semis, investors are favoring proven scale and clear exposure to advanced nodes and AI workloads, while being more selective around newer or niche names that came to market during the peak of AI enthusiasm. Diversification across the value chain – from design software to connectivity to foundry – remains a prudent approach.

### Data And Analytics: Datadog (DDOG), Snowflake (SNOW), MongoDB (MDB), Amplitude (AMPL), And Dynatrace (DT)

In data and analytics, Datadog’s roughly twelve percent weekly gain and modest positive monthly performance contrast with Snowflake’s roughly eight percent weekly gain but about twelve percent monthly decline and MongoDB’s roughly seven percent weekly gain with a mid‑single‑digit monthly pullback. Amplitude’s roughly twelve percent weekly decline and nearly thirty eight percent monthly drop, along with Dynatrace’s roughly ten percent weekly gain but mid‑single‑digit monthly decline, highlight the dispersion within the cohort.

Investors appear to be rewarding platforms with clear product breadth, strong net retention, and proven ability to expand within customers – attributes that favor Datadog, Snowflake, and MongoDB – while penalizing smaller, more narrowly focused analytics vendors when growth slows or go‑to‑market execution lags. Amplitude’s drawdown suggests concerns around the durability of product analytics demand and competition, while Dynatrace’s recent volatility likely reflects its positioning between infrastructure monitoring and observability, where competition is intense.

For portfolios, the data and analytics space remains a core area of secular growth, but position sizing and name selection are critical. Allocating capital to category leaders while opportunistically trading around valuation extremes in second‑tier names can help balance risk and reward.

### Consumer Staples: McCormick (MKC), Clorox (CLX), Kimberly‑Clark (KMB), And Keurig Dr Pepper (KDP)

Consumer staples on the watchlist provided a measure of stability, with McCormick up roughly six percent on the week and more than four percent on the month, Clorox up about five to six percent on the week and around thirteen percent on the month, Kimberly‑Clark ahead by nearly five percent on the week, and Keurig Dr Pepper up about four to five percent on the week. These moves, while modest compared to the volatility seen in growth and cyclical names, illustrate the role that staples continue to play as defensive ballast in portfolios.

Investors appear to be rewarding staples with strong brands, pricing power, and improving cost structures, even as they remain mindful of valuation. In a market where many growth names are undergoing sharp multiple compression, the relative appeal of stable earnings and dividends increases, particularly for investors with lower risk tolerance. The challenge is that as more capital seeks safety in staples, valuations can become stretched, limiting forward returns. Still, the recent performance suggests that in the current environment, the market is comfortable paying a reasonable premium for resilience.

## Upcoming Catalysts

With no earnings on the watchlist over the next two weeks, upcoming catalysts will skew toward macro data releases, policy developments, and any unscheduled corporate actions such as M&A, regulatory decisions, or strategic updates. For sectors like fintech, financials, and consumer, incremental data on employment, inflation, and consumer sentiment will influence expectations for credit quality, spending, and rate paths, thereby affecting names such as LPL, Block, Affirm, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, JPMorgan, and Capital One.

In technology, any news flow around AI infrastructure spending plans from hyperscalers, cloud providers, or large enterprises will be pivotal for names like Vertiv, Corning, Taiwan Semiconductor, Cadence, and related semis. Similarly, incremental updates from cloud platforms or large software vendors on enterprise IT budgets, AI adoption, and digital transformation roadmaps could have knock‑on effects for software infrastructure and application names, from Fastly and Cloudflare to monday.com, Freshworks, and ServiceNow, which gained about six percent this week but remains down roughly twenty percent on the month.

For ad‑supported and consumer internet platforms such as Pinterest, Netflix, Sprinklr, Zeta, and others, evolving narratives around digital ad budgets, user engagement, and competition across platforms will remain key drivers. Any evidence of stabilization in ad demand or improved monetization could catalyze short‑covering and re‑rating, particularly after the steep monthly drawdowns seen in Pinterest and peers. Conversely, negative headlines or guidance from major advertisers could further pressure the group.

Finally, regulatory and policy developments, whether related to financial regulation, data privacy, antitrust, or sector‑specific issues such as healthcare and telehealth, will be important for names like Hims & Hers, Block, Affirm, and larger platforms beyond the watchlist. In the absence of earnings, even incremental policy signals can move stocks significantly when positioning is stretched.

## What To Watch Next Week

As we look ahead to next week, the dominant themes across the watchlist are likely to remain factor rotation, dispersion within sectors, and the ongoing tug‑of‑war between long‑duration growth and real‑asset or cash‑flow‑rich exposures. Within technology, watch for signs of follow‑through or reversal in the software infrastructure cohort, particularly Fastly, Vertiv, Akamai, Cloudflare, and DigitalOcean, which gained about eight percent on the week and nearly twenty nine percent on the month. A second week of strong performance could cement a narrative shift toward profitable infrastructure and edge names, while a quick reversal would argue for the moves being more technical than fundamental.

In application software and SaaS, monitoring whether the heavy drawdowns in monday.com, Freshworks, Asana, Tyler Technologies, Cognizant, Intuit, Atlassian, and Veeva, which fell about five percent on the week and more than twenty percent on the month, start to attract value and growth buyers will be important. Stabilization in this cohort, even without a sharp rebound, would signal that the de‑rating phase may be nearing exhaustion. Conversely, continued weakness could set up a more extended reset in how investors value even high‑quality cloud software.

For cybersecurity, watch the behavior of Rapid7, Varonis, CrowdStrike, Rubrik, Tenable, Zscaler, Qualys, and Check Point. Any signs of renewed selling in Rapid7 could spill over to other mid‑tier security names, while sustained relative strength in CrowdStrike and Tenable would reinforce the preference for scale and profitability. In semis, the key watchpoints will be whether Astera Labs can stabilize after its steep declines, whether Intel continues to lag, and whether Taiwan Semiconductor maintains its leadership as a core AI and advanced node exposure.

Within fintech and financials, tracking flows and price action in LPL, Block, Affirm, Wells Fargo, Bank of America, JPMorgan, Capital One, Global Payments, Synchrony, and Shift4 will help gauge whether the market is becoming more constructive on consumer and credit risk or remains in de‑risking mode. A stabilization or modest rebound in these names would suggest that investors believe the bulk of the de‑rating is behind them, while further weakness could signal rising concern about macro and credit.

Finally, in energy, industrials, and materials, watch whether Generac, Vertiv, Comfort Systems, Corning, Agnico Eagle, Newmont, and Caterpillar can sustain their strong momentum. Continued outperformance here would reinforce the view that real‑asset‑linked names will be core leadership in this phase of the cycle, while any sharp reversal might indicate that the recent moves have been overextended. For diversified portfolios, the interplay between these groups and higher‑beta growth names will drive performance and shape the opportunity set for adding or trimming risk.

Overall, the week ahead is likely to be characterized by high dispersion, ongoing multiple recalibration, and an elevated role for technicals and flows given the absence of near‑term earnings. Maintaining flexibility, emphasizing quality within each sector, and being deliberate about where to take duration and valuation risk will be critical as the market continues to digest the implications of the current macro and policy regime for our watchlist names.

market_summary: US equities saw pronounced factor and sector dispersion this week despite limited incremental macro data, with high-beta software and select industrials sharply diverging from large-cap benchmarks. Index performance cannot be quantified here, but the tape reflected a pickup in single-name volatility, particularly across cloud, cybersecurity, and fintech, while defensives like staples and gold-linked miners found support. Within tech, cloud infrastructure outperformed on violent squeezes in crowded shorts such as FSLY and rotation into data center–levered names like VRT, while application software and certain fintechs sold off hard on profit-taking and positioning resets. Looking ahead, the market’s focus turns to the next inflation and Fed signals, as well as whether this week’s sharp reversals in software and cyclicals mark the start of a broader factor rotation or just a short-covering interlude.
